# Introduction

I want to determine a humbly-optimized strategy for my long-term investment portfolio. My goal is to maximize the [utility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utility) I will derive from this portfolio. Assuming constant relative risk aversion and a utility function of the following form, as per [Merton's portfolio problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merton's_portfolio_problem):

$$
u(x) = \frac{x^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}
$$

where

- $u(x)$ is the utility derived from an $x$ level of wealth (which is consumed to produce utility)
- $x$ is the amount of wealth consumed
- and $\gamma$ is a constant measuring the level of risk aversion

I estimated that, personnally, $\gamma = 2$. This estimation is out of the scope of this study, see Haghani & White ([2018](https://elmwealth.com/measuring-the-fabric-of-felicity/)) for an introduction.

@fig-crra-utility shows the shape of my utility function: utility rises with consumed wealth but with decreasing marginal return, and $\gamma$ sets how fast that marginal rate of return decays.

```{python}
#| label: fig-crra-utility
#| fig-cap: "CRRA utility of consumed wealth, for my $\\gamma = 2$ and two other risk aversion levels, for comparison. (Utility is ordinal, only the shape of the curve is meaningful, not the absolute values. And values cannot be compared across distinct functions like the three above.)"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

x = np.linspace(0.5, 5, 400)
crra_gammas = [(1.5, "#E69F00", 1.2), (2.0, "#0072B2", 2.2), (3.0, "#009E73", 1.2)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for gamma, color, linewidth in crra_gammas:
    ax.plot(
        x,
        x ** (1 - gamma) / (1 - gamma),
        color=color,
        linewidth=linewidth,
        label=f"γ = {gamma:g}",
    )
ax.set_xlim(x.min(), x.max())
ax.set_ylim(-3, 0.15)
ax.set_xlabel("Wealth consumed, x")
ax.set_ylabel("Utility, u(x)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, loc="lower right")
ax.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

I am designing this strategy to be implemented in an [Interactive Brokers (IBKR) *compte-titre ordinaire* (CTO)](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/accounts/individual.php?menu=B) as a French citizen. This choice implies that I would have access to a wide array of instruments.

I have already defined the universe of assets I will consider and submit to the optimization (all EUR-denominated):

- an [MSCI ACWI](https://www.msci.com/indexes/index/892400/msci-acwi-index) ETF;
- a US Treasury 7-10 year bond ETF, EUR-hedged, such as [CEMF](https://www.justetf.com/en/etf-profile.html?isin=IE000K1VI152);
- a [managed futures](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/White-Papers/Understanding-Managed-Futures) ETF such as [DBMFE](https://www.imgp.com/fund/LU2951555403-imgp-dbi-managed-futures-fund-r-eur-ucits-etf/) (ideally, several ones to diversify the manager risk);
- and a gold ETF.

The definition of this universe is out of scope but was inspired, between others, by Ilmanen ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198)).

An IBKR CTO allows the implementation of short box spreads for fixed-rate, low-cost leverage. The derivation of the properties of this combination of options is fascinating but also kept out of the scope of this study, see [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Box_spread).

Analytical process:

- I will first define the inputs of the optimizer -- the assets' expected return, volatility and correlation. This step is very challenging, hence, I will employ techniques designed to keep those estimates humble and as evidence-based as possible.
- I will then run mean-variance optimization (MVO) on those inputs to identify the [tangency portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory#Tangency_portfolio), as per the modern portfolio theory. MVO being theoretically exact but practically very sensitive to the fraction of error in the inputs, I will correct this result by tilting the assets' weights toward a conservative anchor.
- I will then solve for the amount of leverage to apply to this optimized portfolio to maximize utility. The challenge is to estimate the portfolio of assets that will maximize the expected return per unit of risk taken, and then leverage it to the level of risk that best suits my psychology (@eq-challenge).
- But because unconstrained, utility-maximizing leveraging ignores the risk of forced liquidation (given IBKR's margin requirements), I will cap it at the level that keeps that risk low enough and check whether, once leverage is constrained, the optimal composition shifts away from the tangency.

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\text{return}}{\text{risk}}}_{\text{to maximize}} \times \underbrace{\text{leverage}}_{\substack{\text{to adapt to my} \\ \text{risk aversion level}}}
$$ {#eq-challenge}

# Computing the inputs of the mean-variance optimizer
## Covariance matrix
### Historical covariances & Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage

```{python}
#| label: ledoit-wolf
import numpy as np

from covariance import ledoit_wolf_covariance, correlation

cov_lw, delta = ledoit_wolf_covariance(returns)
lw_delta_fmt = f"{delta:.2f}"

# Shrinkage target: the average of the off-diagonal sample correlations.
sample_corr = returns.corr()
off_diagonal = ~np.eye(len(sample_corr), dtype=bool)
avg_corr_fmt = f"{sample_corr.values[off_diagonal].mean():.2f}"
```

The sample of historical returns allows us to compute a covariance matrix. But, as per Ledoit & Wolf ([2003](http://www.ledoit.net/honey.pdf)), "nobody should be using the sample
covariance matrix for the purpose of portfolio optimization" because of its estimation error. As such, our sample covariance matrix is shrunk toward a constant-correlation target with the optimal shrinkage constant $\delta$ set to `{python} lw_delta_fmt` by the Ledoit-Wolf estimator^[The problem targetted by Ledoit & Wolf is most important in cases where the number of assets surpasses the number of observations in each return time series which is far from our case, but I apply that method for robustness.]. That results in each pair-wise correlation coefficient to be pulled toward the average sample pair-wise correlation coefficient (@tbl-shrinkage).

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shrinkage
#| tbl-cap: "Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk correlations; each off-diagonal cell shows the shrunk value, with the shift from the sample correlation in parentheses."
_shrunk = correlation(cov_lw)
_shift = _shrunk - returns.corr()
_cells = _shrunk.copy().astype(object)
for _i in _shrunk.index:
    for _j in _shrunk.columns:
        _cells.loc[_i, _j] = (
            "1.00"
            if _i == _j
            else f"{_shrunk.loc[_i, _j]:.2f} ({round(_shift.loc[_i, _j], 2) + 0.0:+.2f})"
        )
mask_upper(_cells)
```

The shifts shown in parentheses in @tbl-shrinkage are small, so that the pull toward the `{python} avg_corr_fmt` average correlation is mild.


### Regime inspection

The correlations above -- sample or shrunk -- are full-period averages.
They hide the evolution of the degree of comovement over time between the sleeve proxies.
To be more specific, I want equities to be un- or anticorrelated relative to the other sleeves when equities crash. An average correlation doesn't provide enough time granularity to examine this.
So it is important that we scrutinize those single numbers before feeding them to MVO. In @tbl-regime-corr, I bucket the `{python} n_months` months of data by the sign of their equity return and compute each sleeve's correlation with equity within each bucket.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-regime-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Correlation with equity by equity-state bucket."
from regimes import conditional_correlations

cc = conditional_correlations(returns)
trend_up_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity up', 'trend']:.2f}"
trend_down_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity down', 'trend']:.2f}"
trend_worst_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity worst quartile', 'trend']:.2f}"
gold_worst_fmt = f"{cc.loc['equity worst quartile', 'gold']:.2f}"

(
    cc.rename_axis("equity state")
    .reset_index()
    .style.hide(axis="index")
    .format(precision=2)
)
```

@tbl-regime-corr shows that:

- Bonds acted as a risk-off hedge: negatively correlated with equity throughout, and increasingly so as equity weakens -- deepest in its worst quartile (@tbl-regime-corr).
- Trend acted as a convex hedge: mildly positively-correlated with equity when equity rises (`{python} trend_up_fmt`), but turning slightly negatively-correlated when equity falls (`{python} trend_down_fmt` to `{python} trend_worst_fmt`).
- Gold acted as a tail hedge: roughly uncorrelated when equity rises or falls modestly, but negatively-correlated (`{python} gold_worst_fmt`) in the worst quartile.

The buckets in @tbl-regime-corr pool months regardless of when they occured. @fig-rolling-corr instead shows how equity correlated with the other sleeves over time.

```{python}
colors = {"bonds": "#0072B2", "trend": "#009E73", "gold": "#E69F00"}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for sleeve in roll.columns:

ax.axhline(0, color="0.6", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Correlation with equity")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
```

@fig-rolling-corr provides additional insights:

- As the [headlines](https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Perspectives/A-Positive-Stock-Bond-Correlation-Is-a-Terrible-Reason-to-Add-More-Equity-Risk-to-Your-Portfolio) said, the stock-bond correlation turned positive. Negative for most of the period, it flipped sign around 2022 and remained elevated into 2025 (@fig-rolling-corr). The risk-off hedge of the 2000s and 2010s has, for now, become a risk-on co-mover.
- Trend's correlation to stocks swings widely (from +0.76 in 2006 to -0.35 in 2024), consistent with its convex, regime-dependent behavior.
- And gold's was most stable (-0.33 to +0.39), albeit rarely substantially anticorrelated.


### The final covariance

The regime inspection flags one correlation to scrutinise: the equity-bonds one. For the EUR-hedged US Treasury sleeve it is genuinely negative -- a structural, rates-driven flight-to-quality decorrelation, and the very property the sleeve was chosen for (@tbl-regime-corr): hedged Treasuries rallied while equities fell through the GFC and Covid. It is not an all-weather hedge, though: it turned positive in the 2022 inflation shock, when bonds and equities fell together, and the rolling correlation was still elevated at the sample end (@fig-rolling-corr).

An earlier, unhedged version of this study distrusted this pair and overrode it toward zero. I no longer do. That distrust fit a sleeve whose negative correlation rested on an unhedged dollar cushion that might not recur; the hedged sleeve's decorrelation is instead the rates flight-to-quality that is its raison d'être, so overriding it away would contradict the choice to hold it. Its one failure mode -- the inflation regime, where no government bond hedges equities -- is real, but covering it is the job of the gold and trend sleeves, not something I patch by distorting this input. I therefore feed MVO the Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk correlation directly (@tbl-final-corr); the shrinkage already pulls the raw estimate toward the cross-sleeve average, a principled temper in place of a hand-set number.

The bond volatility is likewise left at its sample value (@tbl-final-vol): the EUR-hedged sleeve carries the rate volatility of 7-10y Treasuries with the currency stripped out, so there is nothing to correct.

The non-equity sleeves' crisis-hedging value is convex and state-dependent, which is an information a single covariance matrix cannot convey. Editing the correlations cannot capture it. MVO prices these sleeves on their average comovement, so it under-weights the tail protection they offer. This is a known limitation of any single-covariance optimizer, which I accept.

What MVO is fed is the covariance matrix $\Sigma$: its diagonal holds the sleeve variances (the volatilities squared) and its off-diagonal entries are $\Sigma_{ij} = \sigma_i\,\sigma_j\,\rho_{ij}$. @tbl-final-corr and @tbl-final-vol decompose it into correlations and volatilities for legibility.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-final-corr
#| tbl-cap: "Final correlation matrix (Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk, used as-is)."
from covariance import annualized_vols, final_covariance

cov_final = final_covariance(returns)
mask_upper(correlation(cov_final).map("{:.2f}".format))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-final-vol
#| tbl-cap: "Final annualized volatilities (sample; no override)."
(
    pd.DataFrame({"annualized vol": annualized_vols(cov_final).map("{:.1%}".format)})
    .rename_axis("sleeve")
    .reset_index()
    .style.hide(axis="index")
)
```


## Expected returns

The second MVO input is the vector of expected returns -- the least reliable estimates, and one of the inputs MVO is most sensitive to. So, rather than feeding my own point estimates directly, I pass them through a Black-Litterman model (He & Litterman, [2002](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=334304); [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black%E2%80%93Litterman_model)): it starts with the market-implied returns (more on that below), considered as a reasonable anchor (playing the role of a Bayesian prior), and tilts them toward my personal views using a given confidence level I also provide.


### The equilibrium prior

The market-implied return is the equilibrium return of the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM; Sharpe, [1964](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1964.tb02865.x)), recovered by reverse optimization. A mean-variance investor with risk-aversion coefficient $\delta$ ($\lambda$ in Idzorek's notation) chooses risky-asset weights $w$ to maximize the quadratic utility $U(w) = w'\Pi - \tfrac{\delta}{2}\,w'\Sigma w$, where $\Pi$ is the vector of expected excess returns over the risk-free rate and $\Sigma$ their covariance matrix. Its first-order condition, $\Pi - \delta\Sigma w = 0$, gives the optimal weights $w = \tfrac{1}{\delta}\Sigma^{-1}\Pi$ (Markowitz, [1952](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-6261.1952.tb01525.x)). Reverse optimization inverts this relation: taking the capitalization-weighted market portfolio $w_\text{mkt}$ as optimal, the excess returns that justify holding it are

$$
\Pi = \delta\,\Sigma\,w_\text{mkt}
$$

the implied equilibrium returns (Idzorek, [2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075068321-0.50003-0)), where $w_\text{mkt}$ is the vector of market-capitalization weights. Adding the risk-free rate gives the expected return reported in @tbl-bl-prior.

The weights $w_\text{mkt}$ are the market capitalizations normalized to sum to one, which treats the four sleeves as the whole market. They are not -- credit, real estate, cash and many other assets are excluded -- but computing the equilibrium over the investable universe rather than a literally global market portfolio is the standard Black-Litterman construction, in which the market is the set of assets under consideration (He & Litterman, [1999](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=334304); Idzorek, [2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075068321-0.50003-0)). The prior is thus the CAPM-implied return within that universe. @tbl-bl-prior shows the capitalizations (in USD for data availability; only the ratios matter, so the currency is irrelevant), the implied weights, and the prior:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bl-prior
#| tbl-cap: "Market capitalizations, the implied market weights, and the equilibrium prior Π (real)."
import black_litterman as bl
from black_litterman import MARKET_CAPS, market_weights
from mu import RF_REAL

bl_prior = bl.equilibrium_prior(cov_final)
bl_delta = bl.market_delta(cov_final)
bl_delta_fmt = f"{bl_delta:.1f}"
cap_equity_fmt = f"{MARKET_CAPS['equity']:.0f}"
cap_bonds_fmt = f"{MARKET_CAPS['bonds']:.0f}"
cap_gold_fmt = f"{MARKET_CAPS['gold']:.0f}"
trend_vol = cov_final.loc["trend", "trend"] ** 0.5
trend_sharpe = 0.2  # forward net Sharpe assigned to the trend sleeve
trend_sharpe_fmt = f"{trend_sharpe:.1f}"
trend_vol_fmt = f"{trend_vol:.1%}"
rf_real_fmt = f"{RF_REAL:.2%}"
trend_excess_fmt = f"{trend_sharpe * trend_vol:.1%}"
trend_return_fmt = f"{trend_sharpe * trend_vol + RF_REAL:.1%}"
_caps = pd.Series(MARKET_CAPS).reindex(cov_final.index)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "capitalization (USD trillion)": _caps.map(lambda x: "--" if pd.isna(x) else f"{x:,.1f}"),
        "market weight": market_weights(cov_final.index).map("{:.1%}".format),
        "prior Π": bl_prior.map("{:.2%}".format),
    }
).rename_axis("sleeve").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

The capitalizations are the MSCI ACWI free-float market cap (\$`{python} cap_equity_fmt` tn, [MSCI factsheet](https://www.msci.com/documents/10199/255599/msci-acwi-net.pdf), 2026), the US Treasury notes and bonds outstanding (\$`{python} cap_bonds_fmt` tn, [FiscalData MSPD](https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/datasets/monthly-statement-public-debt/summary-of-treasury-securities-outstanding), 2026-07), and WGC financial gold (\$`{python} cap_gold_fmt` tn, [WGC](https://www.gold.org/goldhub/research/market-primer/gold-market-primer-market-size-and-structure), 2026). Managed futures don't have a market capitalization, so they take weight $0$ in the market portfolio. Their equilibrium prior is still not exactly zero, though: the market-implied return depends on each asset's covariance with the market (its $\beta$) rather than on its own weight, and managed futures' low $\beta$ puts them at near-zero prior. Their return therefore comes almost entirely from the view.

The market's risk aversion, $\delta$, is computed based on a set of professional equity risk premium assumptions: I set $\delta$ so that the market-implied return on equity equals that premium, $\delta = \text{ERP} / \operatorname{cov}(\text{equity}, \text{market})$, and every other sleeve's implied return then follows from its covariance with the market -- no separate bond or gold premium is assumed. Equity is ~69 % of the market and the only sleeve with a well-identified premium, so anchoring $\delta$ to it keeps every input sourced. The premium is an external number, not my own equity view (which would make the prior a mirror of it): an arithmetic, over-bills, world equity premium triangulated across the [DMS/UBS 2026 Yearbook](https://www.ubs.com/content/dam/assets/wm/static/cio/documents/giry2026-summary-public.pdf), [Damodaran](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/New_Home_Page/datafile/histimpl.html) (implied US 4.23 %), [Kroll](https://www.kroll.com/en/reports/cost-of-capital/recommended-us-equity-risk-premium-and-corresponding-risk-free-rates) (5.0 %) and the [Fernandez 2026 survey](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6570342) (5.5 %) lands at ~5.0 %. This gives $\delta \approx$ `{python} bl_delta_fmt`. $\delta$ scales the prior's level (and, downstream, the leverage) but not its weights.


### My views

Each sleeve's view is an estimate (partly inspired by Ilmanen's ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198)) asset class-specific methods) fed to the Black-Litterman model with a confidence level (between 0 and 1) representing my degree of trust in the estimate (Idzorek, [2007](https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-075068321-0.50003-0)):

- **Bonds: ~1.0 % real, confidence 0.7.** The ICE US Treasury 7-10y index the sleeve tracks yields 4.60 % to maturity (nominal, USD; [iShares IEF](https://www.ishares.com/us/products/239456/ishares-710-year-treasury-bond-etf), 2026-08). Hedging to EUR gives up the USD-minus-EUR short-rate differential (covered interest parity) -- currently ~1.6 pp (US 1-month 3.78 %, [FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS1MO); €STR 2.19 %, [ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/financial_markets_and_interest_rates/euro_short-term_rate/html/index.en.html)) -- leaving ~3.0 % hedged nominal; minus ~2 % expected inflation ([ECB SPF](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/ecb_surveys/survey_of_professional_forecasters/html/ecb.spf2026q3.en.html)) gives ~1.0 % real. The starting yield is a strong forward predictor of the nominal return and the CAPM prior is a weak model for bonds, so I lean on the view.
- **Equity: 4.03 % real, confidence 0.8.** Elm Wealth's all-world payout-adjusted cyclically-adjusted earnings yield (P-CAEY; White & Haghani, [2024](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4874559)) -- a direct forward real-return estimate -- at 4.03 % ([Elm Wealth](https://elmwealth.com/capital-market-assumptions/), 2026-07-27). It is forward-facing and valuation-aware, whereas the prior is valuation-blind.
- **Trend: ~2.7 % real, confidence 0.65.** A lot of evidence backs the trend premium. It was positive over every decade since 1800 (Lempérière et al., [2014](https://doi.org/10.21314/JOIS.2014.043)), a diversified time-series-momentum Sharpe above 1 since 1966 (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, [2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2011.11.003)), and robust across a century net of fees (Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen, [2017](https://doi.org/10.3905/jpm.2017.44.1.015)). Its existence is well-established; its magnitude is not, though. Those studies' gross Sharpes of 0.7 to >1 come from stronger, less-crowded pre-2000 trends, while the live net-of-fee SG CTA Index I would track via DBMFE had a Sharpe of only ~0.13 over our sample period. I place my view between those bounds. The EUR-unhedged SG CTA that DBMFE benchmarks carries a ~`{python} trend_vol_fmt` volatility; I assign it a forward net Sharpe of `{python} trend_sharpe_fmt`. Its excess real return is then `{python} trend_sharpe_fmt` × `{python} trend_vol_fmt` ≈ `{python} trend_excess_fmt`, and adding the `{python} rf_real_fmt` real cash rate (cf. @sec-leverage) gives `{python} trend_return_fmt` real. The confidence is set below the ones of equity and bonds, and above what a noisy estimate would get, because the CAPM equilibrium prior is structurally unfit here: trend is an anomaly a single-factor model cannot price correctly which penalizes managed futures given their low beta.
- **Gold: no view.** No cashflow and no forward anchor (long-run real return $\approx$ inflation according to Ilmanen ([2022](https://www.wiley.com/en-us/shop/general-finance-investments/investing-amid-low-expected-returns-making-the-most-when-markets-offer-the-least-p-9781119860198))), so I express nothing and leave gold at its equilibrium prior.


### The posterior

The Black-Litterman model blends each view with the prior in inverse proportion to their uncertainties (Idzorek's confidence method, $\tau = 0.05$^[$\tau$ scales the prior's uncertainty level. A small $\tau$ makes the prior harder to depart from. 0.05 is the conventional value.]):

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bl-posterior
#| tbl-cap: "Black-Litterman prior, view, confidence, and posterior μ (real). Gold has no view, so its posterior is the prior."
from black_litterman import VIEW_CONFIDENCES
from mu import VIEWS_REAL

bl_post = bl.posterior_returns(cov_final)
_rows = {}
for _a in cov_final.index:
    _has_view = _a in VIEW_CONFIDENCES
    _rows[_a] = {
        "prior Π": f"{bl_prior[_a]:.2%}",
        "view": f"{VIEWS_REAL[_a]:.2%}" if _has_view else "--",
        "confidence": f"{VIEW_CONFIDENCES[_a]:.1f}" if _has_view else "--",
        "posterior μ": f"{bl_post[_a]:.2%}",
    }
pd.DataFrame(_rows).T.rename_axis("sleeve").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

This posterior is the MVO input. The posterior equity return is not far from my view; bonds also are only modestly shrunk; trend is pulled part-way down from 2.7 % toward its near-zero prior; and gold sits at its prior, equilibrium value.


# Determining the portfolio weights

MVO is fed the posterior $\mu$ (@tbl-bl-posterior) and the covariance $\Sigma$, and outputs the weights of the max-Sharpe portfolio also called the [tangency portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_portfolio_theory#Tangency_portfolio) (@tbl-tangency). The [mutual fund separation theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_fund_separation_theorem#One_risk-free_asset) can then be applied: since borrowing is allowed via short box spreads, any investor's portfolio converges to using the tangency portfolio weights, and scales it using leverage to their own risk aversion level (more on that in the next section; remember @eq-challenge?).

@tbl-mvo-inputs first consolidates what the optimiser sees per sleeve -- posterior excess return, volatility, Sharpe, and correlation with equity -- next to the weight each receives.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-mvo-inputs
#| tbl-cap: "What MVO sees per sleeve: posterior return, volatility, Sharpe, and correlation with equity, next to the resulting tangency weight (real, financed at $R_F$ = 0.19 %)."
from composition import tangency_weights
from mu import RF_REAL

_vols = annualized_vols(cov_final)
_w = tangency_weights(cov_final, bl_post)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "posterior μ": bl_post.map("{:.2%}".format),
        "excess (μ − RF)": (bl_post - RF_REAL).map("{:.2%}".format),
        "ann vol σ": _vols.map("{:.1%}".format),
        "Sharpe": ((bl_post - RF_REAL) / _vols).map("{:.2f}".format),
        "corr w/ equity": correlation(cov_final)["equity"].map("{:.2f}".format),
        "tangency weight": _w.map("{:.1%}".format),
    }
).rename_axis("sleeve").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tangency
#| tbl-cap: "The tangency portfolio: max-Sharpe of the Black-Litterman model's posterior returns and of the covariance matrix (real, financed at $R_F$ = 0.19 %)."
from composition import portfolio_performance, tangency_weights

w_risky = tangency_weights(cov_final, bl_post)
r_risky, s_risky, sh_risky = portfolio_performance(w_risky, bl_post, cov_final)
_row = {f"{sleeve} weight": f"{weight:.1%}" for sleeve, weight in w_risky.items()}
_row.update({"E[r]": f"{r_risky:.1%}", "σ": f"{s_risky:.1%}", "Sharpe": f"{sh_risky:.2f}"})
tang_vol_fmt = f"{s_risky:.0%}"
w_equity_fmt = f"{w_risky['equity']:.0%}"
w_bonds_fmt = f"{w_risky['bonds']:.0%}"
w_trend_fmt = f"{w_risky['trend']:.0%}"
w_gold_fmt = f"{w_risky['gold']:.0%}"
pd.DataFrame([_row]).style.hide(axis="index")
```


# Applying leverage {#sec-leverage}

The tangency portfolio's volatility (~`{python} tang_vol_fmt`) is far below the risk I should bear given its Sharpe. Financing at a real rate $R_F$ -- my box-spread cost, ~0.19 % real^[Box spreads finance at ~the EUR risk-free curve at their tenor. Rolling quarterly, that tenor is ~3 months, well approximated by the overnight €STR of 2.19 % ([ECB](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/stats/financial_markets_and_interest_rates/euro_short-term_rate/html/index.en.html), 2026-07-24); minus ~2 % expected inflation gives ~0.19 % real. The truest figure is the implied rate of my own box fills each quarter -- this is the ex-ante proxy.] -- a CRRA investor with risk aversion $\gamma$ holds a fraction $k^* = S / (\gamma\,\sigma)$ of wealth in the tangency portfolio, where $S = (\mu_p - R_F)/\sigma$ is its excess Sharpe and $\sigma$ its volatility. That implies a target volatility $\sigma^* = S/\gamma$ and an expected real return $R_F + S^2/\gamma$; $k^* > 1$ is gross leverage, financed by short box spreads at ~$R_F$.

```{python}
#| label: leverage-calc
#| include: false
from leverage import (
    GAMMA,
    levered_allocation,
    levered_expected_return,
    optimal_leverage,
    target_volatility,
)

k = optimal_leverage(sh_risky, s_risky, GAMMA)
k_fmt = f"{k:.2f}:1"
sstar_fmt = f"{target_volatility(sh_risky, GAMMA):.1%}"
erlev_fmt = f"{levered_expected_return(sh_risky, GAMMA):.1%}"
```

At $\gamma = 2$ that is a gross exposure of `{python} k_fmt`, a target volatility of `{python} sstar_fmt`, and an expected real return of `{python} erlev_fmt`. @tbl-leverage shows the resulting book as fractions of NAV: the financing leg (`borrowed cash`) is the box-spread borrowing.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leverage
#| tbl-cap: "The tangency portfolio levered to the CRRA optimum (γ = 2), % of NAV."
pd.DataFrame(
    {"% NAV": (levered_allocation(w_risky, k) * 100).round(0).astype(int).astype(str) + " %"}
).rename_axis("position").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index")
```

The resulting $k^*$ is `{python} k_fmt`. But this is the unconstrained optimum, and a practical cap (portfolio margin, box-spread capacity) may bind below $k^*$ and would tilt the book away from the low-vol sleeves. The real financing rate above already trims $k^*$; any box-spread spread over the risk-free would trim it a little more. @tbl-leverage-gamma shows the sensitivity to $\gamma$.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-leverage-gamma
#| tbl-cap: "Leverage, target volatility, and expected real return vs. risk aversion γ."
rows = {}
for g in [1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0]:
    rows[g] = {
        "k* (leverage)": f"{optimal_leverage(sh_risky, s_risky, g):.2f}:1",
        "σ* (target vol)": f"{target_volatility(sh_risky, g):.1%}",
        "E[r] real": f"{levered_expected_return(sh_risky, g):.1%}",
    }
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.rename_axis("γ").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=1)
```


# Margin-call stress test {#sec-stress}

```{python}
#| label: stress-setup
#| include: false
import stress
from data import daily_returns_matrix

returns_daily = daily_returns_matrix()
daily_start = f"{returns_daily.index.min():%Y-%m}"
daily_f = stress.ESTR_NOMINAL + 0.005  # base case: €STR + 0.5 %
daily_path = stress.simulate_path(
    returns_daily, w_risky, k, 0.0, daily_f, 63, periods_per_year=252
)
rho0_fmt = f"{1 / k:.1%}"
kstar_fmt = f"{k:.2f}"
daily_min_rho_fmt = f"{daily_path.ratio.min():.1%}"
daily_min_rho_date = f"{daily_path.ratio.idxmin():%Y-%m}"
covid_rho_fmt = f"{daily_path.ratio.loc['2020-02':'2020-04'].min():.1%}"

# One daily bootstrap, reused for the table (@tbl-stress-boot) and the prose below.
_boot = stress.bootstrap_grid(
    returns_daily, w_risky, k, spreads=(0.005,), rebalances=stress.DAILY_REBALANCE,
    bootstrap="stationary", block=63, periods_per_year=252, n_paths=2000,
)
_q25 = _boot[(_boot["rebalance"] == "quarterly") & (_boot["m"] == "25%")].iloc[0]
pcall25_fmt = _q25["P(call) 30y"]
dd_med_fmt = _q25["DD (median)"].lstrip("-")
dd_p5_fmt = _q25["DD (5th pct)"].lstrip("-")
```

The leverage above follows from my risk aversion; this section answers the separate question any levered strategy must face -- what is the drawdown and margin-call risk -- and answers it out of sample, by pushing the chosen book through history and through bootstrapped paths it was never fit to.

A margin call here is specific. Box-spread financing is a fixed-term loan: the lender cannot pull it or reprice it mid-crisis, which is its advantage over a margin loan. But the borrowed cash buys marked-to-market ETFs, and Interactive Brokers still liquidates if account equity falls below the maintenance requirement on those longs. Normalising net asset value to 1 at gross leverage $k$, with gross book $G_t = \sum_i P_{i,t}$, a loan $L_t$ that accrues the financing rate, and $NAV_t = G_t - L_t$, the margin ratio is $\rho_t = NAV_t / G_t$ and a call fires when $\rho_t < m$, the maintenance ratio. The book starts at $\rho_0 = 1/k =$ `{python} rho0_fmt`.

The test is deliberately severe, and run daily: month-end marks would miss the intra-month spikes -- a crash like March 2020 falls and partly rebounds inside a single month -- so the daily path is the credible version. I monitor daily with no preventive deleveraging between rebalances, so the book drifts to higher effective leverage after losses; I reset to the target $k$ and weights quarterly (my plan) or annually (the longest unmanaged drift); and I finance at the overnight €STR plus a pessimistic 0.5 % or 1 %, compounded. A margin call is a nominal event and the sleeve series are nominal, so the loan accrues at a nominal rate rather than the study's real $R_F$. The daily window reaches back to `{python} daily_start` -- set by the IEF-based bond sleeve -- covering the GFC, the March-2020 crash and the 2022 sell-off at daily resolution.

What maintenance ratio applies? Interactive Brokers margins European accounts on a risk-based portfolio model by default ([IBKR stocks](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-stocks.php?hm=eu&ex=eu&rgt=0&rsk=1&pm=0&rst=040404040404040104), [bonds](https://www.interactivebrokers.ie/en/trading/margin-bonds.php?hm=eu&ex=eu&rgt=0&rsk=1&pm=0&rst=040404040404040104)), but UCITS funds and ETFs carry a 25 % maintenance requirement, so a book built entirely from UCITS ETFs sits at about 25 %. I take DBMFE at the same 25 % UCITS baseline. The grid brackets the realistic requirement (25 %) with two stress levels (30 %, 35 %) that stand in for the risk-based model tightening procyclically in a crisis.

@tbl-stress-crisis pushes the actual daily path through each crisis; the drawdown and the lowest margin ratio are independent of $m$, so the ratio is read straight against the three thresholds. @tbl-stress-hist runs the full daily window across the grid, @fig-stress plots it, and @tbl-stress-boot bootstraps thirty-year paths from it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stress-crisis
#| tbl-cap: "The levered book through each crisis (daily): peak-to-trough drawdown and the lowest margin ratio reached (to compare against 25 / 30 / 35 %). Quarterly resets, €STR + 0.5 %."
stress.crisis_report(
    returns_daily, w_risky, k, daily_f, 63,
    crises=stress.DAILY_CRISES, periods_per_year=252,
).style.hide(axis="index")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stress-hist

stress.historical_grid(
    returns_daily, w_risky, k, spreads=(0.005,),
    rebalances=stress.DAILY_REBALANCE, periods_per_year=252,
).drop(columns="financing").style.hide(axis="index")
```

The daily record is less comfortable than the leverage alone suggests. On the realised path the margin ratio bottoms at `{python} daily_min_rho_fmt` (`{python} daily_min_rho_date`, the March-2020 crash; @fig-stress, @fig-stress-covid): it never quite reached the 25 % UCITS line historically, but it fell clean through the 30 % and 35 % stress levels, so a book held at those maintenances would have been called (@tbl-stress-hist).

The bootstrap is starker still (@tbl-stress-boot). Over thirty-year paths, even the realistic 25 % UCITS maintenance is called in `{python} pcall25_fmt` of runs, and the 30 % and 35 % stress levels in essentially all of them: the realised history simply did not draw the one adverse sequence that a reset fails to interrupt, but the resampled paths do. The drawdown is severe whether or not a call fires -- the median thirty-year path draws down about `{python} dd_med_fmt`, with a fifth-percentile tail near `{python} dd_p5_fmt`.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-stress-boot
#| tbl-cap: "Daily stationary-bootstrap 30-year paths (2000 runs, mean block ~63 trading days): probability of a margin call, and the median and fifth-percentile worst drawdown. €STR + 0.5 %."
_boot.drop(columns="financing").style.hide(axis="index")
```

So at the CRRA-optimal $k =$ `{python} kstar_fmt` the margin call is not a remote tail: a roughly one-in-four chance over thirty years even at the maintenance I actually face. The leverage that maximises my utility is silent on this, because utility prices drawdown but not the absorbing event of a forced liquidation. The next section adds the constraint it leaves out.


# Margin-aware leverage {#sec-margin-aware}

```{python}
#| label: margin-aware-calc
#| include: false
from constrained import (
    composition_sweep,
    critical_leverages,
    historical_breach_leverage,
    margin_call_probability,
    ruin_safe_leverage,
)

crit = critical_leverages(returns_daily, w_risky, maintenance=0.25)
k_margin = float(np.percentile(crit, 5))
p_call_kstar = margin_call_probability(crit, k)
p_call_kmargin = margin_call_probability(crit, k_margin)

er_tan = r_risky - RF_REAL  # tangency excess real return


def _J(kk, g=GAMMA):
    return RF_REAL + kk * er_tan - 0.5 * g * (kk * s_risky) ** 2


def _Er(kk):
    return RF_REAL + kk * er_tan


kstar_fmt = f"{k:.2f}"
k_margin_fmt = f"{k_margin:.2f}"
pcall_kstar_fmt = f"{p_call_kstar:.0%}"
pcall_km_fmt = f"{p_call_kmargin:.0%}"
er_kstar_fmt = f"{_Er(k):.2%}"
er_km_fmt = f"{_Er(k_margin):.2%}"
er_drop_fmt = f"{_Er(k) - _Er(k_margin):.2%}"
k_nohist_fmt = f"{historical_breach_leverage(returns_daily, w_risky):.2f}"
k_margin30_fmt = f"{ruin_safe_leverage(returns_daily, w_risky, maintenance=0.30):.2f}"
```

The leverage in @sec-leverage, $k^* =$ `{python} kstar_fmt`, maximises my CRRA utility -- but that objective prices *drawdown* (through $\gamma$) and not the *absorbing* event that sits right next to it: a forced liquidation. The stress test makes the gap concrete. At $k^*$ the book starts at $\rho_0 = 1/k^* =$ `{python} rho0_fmt`, and run daily through bootstrapped history it breaches the 25 % UCITS maintenance in `{python} pcall_kstar_fmt` of thirty-year paths (@sec-stress). A one-in-four chance of being sold out at the bottom is not a risk my $\gamma$ ever agreed to bear. So I add the constraint the utility function leaves out.

I cap leverage at $k_\text{margin}$: the largest $k$ whose daily-bootstrap probability of *any* margin call (25 % maintenance, quarterly resets) stays within a 5 % ruin budget over thirty years. On this book that is $k_\text{margin} =$ `{python} k_margin_fmt`, and the trade it offers is nearly free (@fig-margin-aware). Trimming from `{python} kstar_fmt` to `{python} k_margin_fmt` cuts the call probability from `{python} pcall_kstar_fmt` to `{python} pcall_km_fmt`, while giving up only `{python} er_drop_fmt` of expected real return (`{python} er_kstar_fmt` to `{python} er_km_fmt`) and *no measurable utility*: $k^*$ sits on the flat top of the utility parabola, so the return I forgo is matched by the variance penalty I save. Ruin risk falls five-fold at a cost of essentially zero.

```{python}
#| label: fig-margin-aware
#| fig-cap: "Utility is flat where ruin is not. CRRA utility $J$ (γ = 2, left) and the 30-year margin-call probability (right) as a function of gross leverage $k$. The unconstrained optimum $k^*$ maximises $J$ but carries a large call probability; trimming to $k_\\text{margin}$ (the 5 % ruin budget, dotted) sheds most of the call risk while $J$ barely moves."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from matplotlib.ticker import PercentFormatter

ks = np.linspace(1.5, 3.6, 120)
Js = np.array([_J(kk) for kk in ks])
pcs = np.array([margin_call_probability(crit, kk) for kk in ks])

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax1.plot(ks, Js, color="#0072B2", linewidth=1.8)
ax1.set_xlabel("Gross leverage $k$")
ax1.set_ylabel("CRRA utility $J$ (γ = 2)", color="#0072B2")
ax1.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#0072B2")
ax1.set_xlim(ks.min(), ks.max())

ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(ks, pcs, color="#CC79A7", linewidth=1.8)
ax2.set_ylabel("P(margin call) over 30y", color="#CC79A7")
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="#CC79A7")
ax2.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1.0))
ax2.axhline(0.05, color="0.6", linewidth=0.8, linestyle=":")

y_txt = ax1.get_ylim()[0] + 0.9 * (ax1.get_ylim()[1] - ax1.get_ylim()[0])
for xk, lab in [(k, "$k^*$"), (k_margin, "$k_\\text{margin}$")]:
    ax1.axvline(xk, color="0.5", linewidth=1.0, linestyle="--")
    ax1.text(xk - 0.02, y_txt, f"{lab} = {xk:.2f}", fontsize=8, color="0.3", ha="right", rotation=90)
ax1.spines[["top"]].set_visible(False)
ax2.spines[["top"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

## Does the cap change the composition? {#sec-tilt}

With unlimited leverage, the mutual-fund separation theorem I invoked when choosing the tangency weights says to hold the tangency and lever it. A binding cap can break that logic: if I cannot reach my risk target by levering the low-volatility tangency, a more equity-heavy book -- higher return, lower Sharpe -- might reach it without hitting the margin wall, and so yield more utility. @tbl-composition-sweep tests this, sweeping the equity weight up from the tangency's `{python} w_equity_fmt`, splitting the remainder among the other sleeves in their tangency proportions, and capping each candidate at its own $k_\text{margin}$.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-composition-sweep
#| tbl-cap: "Composition sweep under the ruin cap. Each row is a book with the given equity weight (remainder split in tangency proportions), capped at its own $k_\\text{margin}$. `γ=1` is the compound-growth (full-Kelly) objective; `γ=2` is my CRRA utility. Growth peaks away from the tangency; utility at γ = 2 does not."
sweep = composition_sweep(cov_final, bl_post, returns_daily, w_risky)
w_eq_growth_fmt = f"{sweep.loc[sweep['growth_g1'].idxmax(), 'w_eq']:.0%}"
w_eq_util_fmt = f"{sweep.loc[sweep['J_g2'].idxmax(), 'w_eq']:.0%}"
(
    pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "equity weight": sweep["w_eq"].map("{:.0%}".format),
            "σ": sweep["sigma"].map("{:.1%}".format),
            "Sharpe": sweep["sharpe"].map("{:.2f}".format),
            "k_margin": sweep["k_margin"].map("{:.2f}".format),
            "γ=2 leverage": sweep["k_g2"].map("{:.2f}".format),
            "γ=2 E[r]": sweep["Er_g2"].map("{:.1%}".format),
            "γ=2 utility J": sweep["J_g2"].map("{:.3f}".format),
            "γ=1 growth": sweep["growth_g1"].map("{:.1%}".format),
        }
    )
    .style.hide(axis="index")
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-composition-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Compound growth (γ = 1) and CRRA utility (γ = 2) across the equity-weight sweep, each book capped at its own $k_\\text{margin}$. Growth is humped -- it rewards tilting toward equity -- while my γ = 2 utility declines monotonically from the tangency (dashed)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(sweep["w_eq"], sweep["growth_g1"], marker="o", color="#009E73", label="compound growth (γ = 1)")
ax.plot(sweep["w_eq"], sweep["J_g2"], marker="o", color="#0072B2", label="CRRA utility $J$ (γ = 2)")
ax.axvline(float(w_risky["equity"]), color="0.5", linewidth=1.0, linestyle="--")
ax.text(float(w_risky["equity"]) + 0.005, ax.get_ylim()[0], " tangency", fontsize=8, color="0.4", va="bottom")
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(xmax=1.0))
ax.set_xlabel("Equity weight")
ax.set_ylabel("Real annual rate")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.grid(True, axis="y", color="0.92")
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

The tilt pays only for a growth-maximiser. Compound growth -- the $\gamma = 1$, full-Kelly objective -- does peak away from the tangency, near an equity weight of `{python} w_eq_growth_fmt`: there the cap binds hard at every composition, so the extra return of a heavier equity book outweighs its lower Sharpe. But at my $\gamma = 2$ the utility-maximising composition is the tangency itself (`{python} w_eq_util_fmt`). My desired leverage `{python} kstar_fmt` already sits essentially at the cap `{python} k_margin_fmt`, so the constraint barely binds and separation survives; tilting toward equity only lowers my utility.

I therefore hold the tangency weights and lever them to $k_\text{margin} =$ `{python} k_margin_fmt`, not the unconstrained `{python} kstar_fmt` -- the same utility for a fifth of the ruin risk. The equity tilt is a tool for a lower risk aversion than mine.

The 5 %-at-25 % rule is a choice, and the cap moves with it. Requiring only that the *realised* history never called lifts it to `{python} k_nohist_fmt` (but one path is a thin guarantee); demanding the 5 % budget against a stressed 30 % maintenance -- IBKR can tighten procyclically -- lowers it to `{python} k_margin30_fmt`.
